name: Underwater
basis: animated sway, colour absorption, caustics, bubbles (how)

lumenary.blurb: The picture seen from below the surface: it sways with the swell, red drains away with depth, nets of light slide over everything, sun rays slant down and bubbles rise. The cursor lets out more bubbles.

facts.bestOn: Bright, colourful scenes with some red in them

why: Water changes light in three ways at once. It bends it, so the view sways with the swell. It absorbs it by colour, red first and blue last, so the deeper you go the bluer and dimmer everything gets. And its rippling surface focuses sunlight into bright moving nets called caustics. Add rays and rising bubbles and the picture is under the sea.
how: Read each pixel from a position pushed about by slow bent waves.
Remove red quickly, green slowly and blue hardly at all, more toward the bottom.
Fog the result toward the colour of the water.
Add three sets of bent ripples and put light where their sum crosses zero.
Draw slanted shafts of sunlight and drifting specks.
Simulate bubbles that rise and wobble, more of them under the cursor.
history: William Thompson took the first underwater photograph in 1856 by lowering a camera in a box into Weymouth Bay. Seventy years later, in 1926, Longley and Martin made the first colour photographs under water for National Geographic, firing magnesium flash powder on a raft because so little red light survives below a few metres. Caustics have been rendered by computer since the 1980s and are still a test of a renderer.
terms: A bright line or patch where a curved surface gathers light.
The loss of light as it passes through a material.
A field that says how far, and which way, to move where each pixel is read from.
paragraphs: Three things happen to light in water, and each is one line of arithmetic per pixel. First, the picture sways. Every output pixel reads the source at a position pushed sideways and up and down by two slow sine waves whose phases are bent by other sines, and blends the four nearest source pixels so straight edges bend smoothly. Second, colour is absorbed. Water takes red first and blue last, so each channel is multiplied by a factor that falls with depth, fastest for red, and the result is fogged toward the water’s own colour. Depth grows toward the bottom of the frame.

Third, caustics. Ripples on the surface act as lenses and gather sunlight into bright lines. Three sets of bent ripples are added together, and light is placed wherever the sum passes through zero; a fourth power thins those crossings into the net seen on the floor of a pool. It is stronger near the top and on bright surfaces. The frame is computed at half size and the sines come from a table of 1024 values, which keeps it at video rate. Sun rays are slanted shafts drawn with additive blending, bubbles are small simulated circles that rise and wobble, and the drifting specks are placed by a formula of time.

equations.note: The swell: where pixel (x, y) is read from. A is the swell slider times 2.2% of the width.
Absorption per channel in tropical water: red is lost about nine times faster than blue. d is the depth slider.
Caustics: f are three bent sine ripples; the net is where their sum is near zero.

presets.text: Open sea at full depth leaves almost only blue.
Strong nets of light in shallow water look like a pool.
A lake is green, still and full of bubbles.
